newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Penguin denies censoring China dissident book in HK.
newsitem.headline: Penguin denies censoring China dissident book in HK.

text.p: The Penguin group on Tuesday dismissed reports that it was imposing self-censorship in Hong Kong on a book by China's top dissident to avoid enraging Beijing just five weeks before China takes over the territory.
Claire Cumming, Penguin's regional marketing and sales manager, said Penguin was promoting the book of essays and letters by jailed dissident Wei Jingsheng like any other book.

Human rights groups voiced concern on Monday after the South China Morning Post newspaper reported the publisher had labelled Wei's writings as too sensitive to promote in Hong Kong. The book is currently available only in the Post's own bookshop.

China will take back the British colony on July 1, and Chinese dissidents living in exile in the territory, along with local pro-democracy activists, have predicted repressive rule after the change of flag. The handover is generating tremendous sensitivity.

There have been signs of self-censorship in the Hong Kong news media in recent months, according to local journalists and politicians, and human rights groups said it would be disturbing if publishers went the same way.

"We've been treating this book as we would every other book," Cumming said, noting it was marketed in the same category as books such as Letters from Burma by Burmese opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
But she added: "Some booksellers were rather cautious about the book and did say they would like to wait and see what the reaction was going to be and other booksellers ordered the book.
"Now that they've sold through, and publicity has been generated, we're getting re-orders. So there should be some quite decent quantities out in the shops.
"There's no reason why Penguin would choose to suppress a book that it's publishing," Cumming said.
The 47-year-old Wei is China's best-known dissident and regarded as the father of China's democracy movement.

He was jailed in 1979 for counter-revolutionary incitement after advocating democratic change and spent 14 and a half years in prison. In 1994 after his release he was detained again and was later sentenced for a further 14 years.
Chinese dissidents abroad arranged publication of Wei's writings in the book, which include strong denunciations of China's leader Deng Xiaoping, who died in February this year.
